question: Where do I hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer?
body:
## Direct Answer

You hire a fractional Chief Revenue Officer through four proven channels: specialized fractional-executive firms (Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional), vetted talent marketplaces (Toptal, Continuum, Graham Weaver style networks), your own investor and board network, and revenue-leader communities like Pavilion or RevGenius. The right channel depends on your stage, budget, and how much vetting you want done for you before the first call.

Finding a fractional CRO is less about locating a person and more about matching a specific revenue problem to a specific operator who has solved it before at your stage. A seed-stage SaaS founder who needs someone to build a first repeatable sales motion should not source from the same pool as a $40M services firm trying to fix a broken forecast. Below is where each channel actually lives, what it costs, how to vet, and the traps that burn founders who hire the wrong fractional leader for the wrong reason.

## What is the fastest place to find a vetted fractional CRO?

The fastest vetted route is a dedicated fractional-executive firm or a curated marketplace, because the screening work is already done. Firms like **Chief Outsiders**, **Bolster**, **Go Fractional**, and **Continuum** maintain benches of pre-interviewed revenue operators and will shortlist two or three matches within days rather than weeks. You pay a premium for that speed and curation, but you skip the months of cold outreach and reference-chasing that a solo search demands.

Marketplaces sit one notch below firms on hand-holding and one notch above raw networking on convenience. On a marketplace you browse profiles, filter by industry and stage, and book intro calls yourself. The tradeoff is real: firms carry more accountability and often guarantee a replacement if the match fails, while marketplaces move faster and cost less but push more of the vetting burden onto you. For a founder who has never hired a revenue executive before, the firm's structured process is usually worth the markup because it forces the scoping conversation that most first-time hirers skip. See our guide to [scoping a fractional revenue engagement](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10241) for the questions to answer before you ever open a search.

There is a subtler reason speed and quality do not have to trade off here, and it is worth understanding before you pick a lane. A firm's bench exists precisely because the firm has already absorbed the cost of a bad hire many times over and encoded what it learned into its intake filter. When you engage Chief Outsiders or Bolster, you are renting the scar tissue of hundreds of prior placements, not just a résumé. That is why a firm can compress a search that would take a founder six weeks into a three-day shortlist without lowering the bar — the bar was raised long before you arrived. The marketplace equivalent is the platform's own reputation data: acceptance rates, repeat-client percentages, and completion history that a raw LinkedIn search will never surface. Treat those signals as the fast lane's version of a reference check, and read them before your first call rather than after.

The honest limitation of the fast channels is that they optimize for the median engagement, not the edge case. If your revenue problem is unusual — a regulated industry, a channel-heavy motion, a hardware-plus-software model, a founder-led sale that needs to be pried loose without breaking momentum — the firm's median-tuned bench may not carry the exact pattern you need. That is the moment to layer a community or network search on top of the fast channel rather than picking one. The two are not mutually exclusive, and the best hirers run them in parallel, using the firm's shortlist as a quality benchmark against which the community candidates are measured.

## Where do fractional CROs actually spend their time between gigs?

The best fractional revenue leaders are rarely on job boards, because they are almost never fully unbooked. They live inside professional communities, and being present where they already gather is the highest-signal channel most founders overlook. **Pavilion** (formerly Revenue Collective) is the flagship community for revenue executives and runs a member directory plus a jobs and fractional board. **RevGenius**, **Modern Sales Pros**, and **Wizards of Ops** carry adjacent talent, especially operators who blend RevOps rigor with frontline sales leadership.

The reason communities beat cold sourcing is trust density. A fractional CRO who is active in Pavilion has a public reputation among peers who will vouch for or warn against them in a single Slack message. When you post a well-scoped need in one of these communities, the responses are pre-filtered by people who have watched each other operate. That social proof is the closest thing to a reference check you can get before the first conversation. It also surfaces the operators who are genuinely good but terrible at self-marketing — the ones who never rank on a marketplace but whose name three separate people drop unprompted.

Community sourcing rewards a specific behavior that most founders skip: contributing before you ask. The operators worth hiring watch how a founder shows up in a shared channel long before they respond to a hiring post. A founder who has answered a few questions, shared a hard-won lesson, or engaged thoughtfully in a thread reads as a good client — someone who will be coachable and candid rather than defensive when the revenue diagnosis stings. The same post from a stranger who appeared only to recruit gets skimmed and ignored. If you are going to source from communities, join a month before you need to hire, not the week of. The lead time is the price of admission, and it pays back in the quality of who replies.

There is also a timing dimension to where fractional leaders spend their between-gig energy. Most good operators run a rolling portfolio of two to four clients, and the natural churn in that portfolio means capacity opens on an irregular but predictable rhythm — an engagement wraps, a client converts to full-time and no longer needs them, a project deliverable ships. Community boards and peer referrals catch that capacity the moment it opens, often before the operator has updated a marketplace profile or told a firm they are available. That is the structural reason the network channel frequently reaches the strongest operators first: it is wired into the informal grapevine that broadcasts availability days before any formal listing does.

The map below shows how the sourcing channels compare on speed, cost, and how much vetting is done for you before you talk to anyone.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[You need a fractional CRO] --> B{How much vetting do you want done}
    B -->|Most done for you| C[Fractional exec firms]
    B -->|Some done for you| D[Curated marketplaces]
    B -->|You do the vetting| E[Communities and network]
    C --> F[Fastest match higher cost]
    D --> G[Fast match medium cost]
    E --> H[Slower match lowest cost highest trust]
    F --> I[Shortlist and scope]
    G --> I
    H --> I
    I --> J[Trial project then engage]
```

## How much does a fractional CRO cost and how does that shape where you look?

Budget is the single biggest filter on where you source, so decide it before you shop. Fractional CROs typically bill in one of three structures: a monthly retainer for a set number of days, an hourly or day rate for project work, or a blended cash-plus-equity arrangement common at early-stage startups. Retainers in the U.S. market generally run from roughly a few thousand dollars a month for light advisory to well into five figures monthly for an operator embedded two to three days a week. Always confirm current rates directly with the person or firm — the range moves with seniority, industry, and scope, and quoting a hard number without a live quote is how engagements start on the wrong foot.

The budget you set steers the channel. A lean startup offering equity-heavy compensation will find better matches through communities and investor networks, where operators are often willing to trade cash for upside in a company they believe in. A funded company that can pay full retainer gets more value from a firm or marketplace, where the premium buys speed, a replacement guarantee, and a curated bench. Trying to source a cash-light equity deal off a premium marketplace, or trying to rush a firm engagement on a shoestring, is the most common mismatch we see. Our breakdown of [fractional versus full-time revenue leadership economics](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10318) walks through the total-cost math so you can size the retainer against the alternative of a full hire.

It helps to separate the two costs hiding inside any fractional retainer: the price of the days and the price of the ramp. The days are what the invoice shows. The ramp is the invisible cost of the operator learning your business, your data, your team, and your buyer before they can move the number — and a fractional leader carries that ramp cost too, just compressed. A good operator will front-load discovery so the ramp is short and visible, often delivering a diagnostic inside the first two weeks. A weaker one lets the ramp stretch quietly across months while billing full retainer, which is why the paid trial matters so much: it forces the ramp to happen on a fixed, cheap clock instead of an open-ended expensive one. When you compare quotes, do not compare day rates alone; compare how fast each operator claims they will produce a first tangible deliverable, because that number, not the rate, determines your real cost per unit of progress.

Equity deserves its own note because founders mishandle it in both directions. Some overpay in equity to land a big name, granting a fractional operator a full-time-sized slice for a two-day-a-week commitment, and then resent it when the engagement tapers. Others underpay, offering a token grant that signals they do not really value the role, and wonder why senior operators pass. The calibration point is that a fractional CRO's equity should reflect the fraction of their time and the length of their expected involvement, with vesting tied to milestones or tenure rather than a cliff designed for a full-time hire. Put the trigger events in writing, define what happens to unvested equity if either side ends the engagement, and agree upfront how a conversion to full-time re-cuts the grant. Ambiguity here is the single most common cause of a good engagement ending badly.

The decision flow below ties budget and stage to the channel that fits.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Set budget and stage] --> B{Can you pay full retainer}
    B -->|Yes funded| C{Need speed and a guarantee}
    B -->|No equity heavy| D[Communities and investor network]
    C -->|Yes| E[Fractional exec firm]
    C -->|No| F[Curated marketplace]
    D --> G[Trial project first]
    E --> G
    F --> G
    G --> H[Scorecard the outcome]
    H --> I{Hit the target}
    I -->|Yes| J[Extend the engagement]
    I -->|No| K[Replace and rescope]
```

## How do I vet a fractional CRO before signing?

Vetting a fractional revenue leader is different from vetting a full-time hire because you are buying a pattern of solved problems, not a career arc. Start by matching stage: an operator who scaled a company from $50M to $200M often cannot build a first repeatable sales motion from zero, and the reverse is just as true. Ask for two or three specific situations that mirror yours — same revenue band, same motion, same buyer — and have them walk you through what they changed, what the number did, and what they would do differently. Vague answers about "driving alignment" without a metric attached are a red flag.

References matter more here than in almost any other hire, because a fractional CRO's entire value is reputation and repeatability. Talk to at least two prior clients, and ask each the same blunt question: would you hire this person again, and for what specifically would you not use them. The best operators are candid about their edges. Finally, insist on a paid trial project — a 30 to 60 day scoped engagement with a concrete deliverable like a rebuilt forecast, a defined sales process, or a diagnosed pipeline leak. A trial reveals working style, communication cadence, and whether they actually move the number, far better than any interview. Pair the trial with a simple scorecard so the go or no-go decision is evidence-based rather than a gut feel; our note on [structuring a revenue-leader trial](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10402) gives a template.

Push past the polished reference to the one nobody offered. Every operator hands you the two clients who will rave; the signal you actually want is in the engagement that did not go well. Ask directly: "Tell me about a client where you were not the right fit — what happened, and how did you handle the exit?" An operator who can narrate a failed engagement with clarity and without blaming the client has both self-awareness and integrity, the two traits that predict how they will behave when your engagement hits its inevitable rough patch. An operator who insists every engagement was a triumph is either inexperienced or editing, and both are disqualifying at this level. The goal of vetting is not to confirm they are good; it is to find the specific shape of their limits so you can decide whether those limits sit anywhere near your problem.

The trial itself should be designed to surface working style, not just output. A rebuilt forecast tells you whether they can model; watching how they run the three meetings it took to build it tells you whether your team will follow them. Sit in on at least one working session during the trial and observe how they handle disagreement from your reps, how they ask for data, and whether they translate their frameworks into your language or force your team into theirs. The deliverable is the visible product of the trial, but the relationship pattern is the thing you are actually buying, because a fractional CRO succeeds or fails on whether the org lets them lead. Score both explicitly on the scorecard so a strong artifact from someone your team quietly rejected does not fool you into a bad extension.

## What red flags mean you are hiring the wrong fractional CRO?

The most expensive mistake is hiring a title instead of a fit. A fractional CRO who is overqualified for your stage will bring frameworks built for a company three sizes larger and quietly stall while your actual bottleneck goes untouched. Watch for operators who lead with methodology jargon and consulting-deck language rather than a crisp diagnosis of your specific revenue problem. If they cannot, in the first call, name the one or two things most likely broken in your funnel, they have not done the homework and probably will not once retained.

The second red flag is overcommitment. Many fractional leaders juggle several clients simultaneously, which is normal and healthy — but ask directly how many, and how they protect your days. Someone carrying eight concurrent engagements cannot be embedded enough to fix a broken revenue org. The third is unwillingness to define success in a number. A serious operator will co-author a target with you before signing — pipeline coverage, win rate, ramp time, forecast accuracy — and will tie the engagement to it. Anyone who resists a measurable outcome is selling presence, not results, and presence is the one thing a fractional hire should never cost you a retainer for.

A fourth red flag is subtler and shows up only after the honeymoon: the operator who builds dependency instead of capability. A fractional CRO's job is ultimately to leave you stronger than they found you — to install a system, coach the team, and document the motion so it survives their departure. Watch for the operator who keeps the forecast logic in their own head, routes every decision through themselves, and makes the org quietly more reliant on their presence each month. That pattern feels like value in the moment and reveals itself as a trap the day they raise the retainer or take on a new client and your revenue engine stalls because nobody else knows how it runs. The right operator is actively working to make themselves less necessary, and will tell you so. Ask in the first call what they intend to leave behind and who on your team they plan to upskill; the answer separates a builder from a rented crutch.

The last red flag is misaligned incentives dressed up as flexibility. Be wary of an operator who resists any structure — no fixed cadence, no defined deliverables, no exit terms, "let's just see how it goes." Flexibility sounds founder-friendly, but at the executive level a refusal to be pinned down usually protects the operator's optionality at your expense, keeping the engagement vague enough that underperformance is never legible. The strongest fractional leaders welcome structure because structure is how they prove their value and earn the renewal. When someone senior pushes back on a scorecard, a cadence, and a clean exit ramp, they are telling you they would rather not be measured, and that is the clearest signal of all that you are looking at the wrong hire.

## Related questions

### What is the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns revenue outcomes and operates inside your org with authority over process, team, and forecast. A consultant advises and hands off recommendations. The CRO stays accountable to the number; the consultant is accountable to the deliverable.

### How many days a week does a fractional CRO work?
Most fractional CRO engagements run one to three days a week, structured as a monthly retainer. Lighter advisory arrangements can be a few hours weekly, while turnaround situations may demand three or more days early on before tapering.

### Can a fractional CRO become full-time later?
Yes, and many engagements are structured with that option. A fractional-to-full-time path lets both sides test fit under real conditions. Agree upfront on how a conversion affects equity, notice, and any firm placement fee.

### Do fractional CROs work with pre-revenue startups?
Rarely and cautiously. Before repeatable revenue exists, the need is usually a founder-led sales motion and product-market-fit work, not a revenue executive. A fractional CRO adds the most value once there is a pipeline to systematize and a team to lead.

### How is a fractional CRO different from a VP of Sales?
A CRO owns the whole revenue system — sales, marketing alignment, RevOps, and forecast — while a VP of Sales owns quota attainment and the sales team. Hire fractional CRO scope when the problem spans functions, not just the sales floor.

### Should the fractional CRO report to me or to the board?
To you, the CEO or founder, always. The operator needs a single accountable line and the authority that comes with reporting to the top. Keep the board informed through you, not through a parallel reporting line that muddies who owns the number.

## FAQ

**How quickly can I get a fractional CRO started?**
Through a firm or marketplace you can be interviewing shortlisted candidates within a week and starting a trial inside two to three weeks. Community and network sourcing takes longer but often yields a stronger cultural match.

**Should I use a firm or hire independently?**
Use a firm if you value speed, a curated bench, and a replacement guarantee, and can pay the premium. Hire independently through communities or your network if you want lower cost, a specific personal match, and are prepared to do your own vetting.

**What should the first engagement deliverable be?**
A concrete diagnostic and one built artifact: a rebuilt forecast, a defined and documented sales process, or a prioritized pipeline-leak fix. Tangible output in the first 30 to 60 days proves the operator moves the number, not just the conversation.

**How do I write a scope that attracts good candidates?**
Lead with the specific revenue problem, your current numbers, the stage, the target outcome, and the time commitment and budget. Strong operators self-select toward clear, honest, metric-anchored scopes and away from vague "help us grow" posts.

**Is equity a normal part of a fractional CRO deal?**
At early-stage startups, yes — a cash-plus-equity blend is common and often necessary to attract senior operators on a lean budget. At funded or later-stage companies, straight cash retainers are the norm. Define vesting and the trigger events in writing.

**What happens if the fractional CRO is not working out?**
If you sourced through a firm, invoke the replacement guarantee. If independent, this is why the paid trial and scorecard exist — a clean 30 to 60 day exit ramp lets you end the engagement on defined terms without the friction of unwinding a full-time hire.

**How do I keep a fractional CRO accountable across a few days a week?**
Co-author a small set of leading and lagging metrics before signing, review them on a fixed weekly cadence, and tie retainer renewal to movement on the target. Accountability is structural, not a matter of hours logged.

**How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?**
Most run six to twelve months, long enough to install a durable revenue system and coach the team, short enough to stay disciplined. Revisit scope quarterly; if the operator has built themselves out of a job, that is success, not a reason to keep paying.

**Can one fractional CRO serve a company with multiple product lines?**
Sometimes, but scope carefully. A single operator can set revenue strategy across lines, but if each line has a distinct motion and buyer, they will spread thin. In that case use the fractional CRO to build the system and hire line-level sales leaders under it.

**Do I need to tell my existing sales team before bringing in a fractional CRO?**
Yes, and frame it as reinforcement, not replacement. Introduce the operator as someone brought in to build the system that makes the team win, name the specific problem they are solving, and give them visible authority so the team engages rather than waits them out.
